title: Claritin and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Loratadine and Claritin-D
excerpt: Can you drink on Claritin? How loratadine and alcohol interact, why Claritin-D needs more care, how it compares to Zyrtec and Benadryl, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Claritin? How loratadine and alcohol interact, why Claritin-D needs extra care, and how it compares to Zyrtec and Benadryl.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most healthy adults, having a drink or two while taking a normal 10 mg dose of Claritin (loratadine) is unlikely to be dangerous. Loratadine is one of the least sedating allergy pills you can buy, and studies at the standard dose have generally not found it adding much to alcohol's effects. "Non-drowsy" doesn't mean "zero drowsiness," though. Some people still feel sleepy on it, alcohol is a sedative, and the combination can catch you off guard. Claritin-D is a different story, because it adds a decongestant called pseudoephedrine that speeds up your heart and raises blood pressure. This guide explains both, plus what Claritin can and can't do for drinking-related stuffiness, flushing, and hangovers.

**The quick rules:** Plain Claritin plus light drinking is generally fine for healthy adults. Don't take more than the labeled dose, because extra loratadine is where drowsiness shows up. Don't drive until you know how the combination affects you. Never stack Claritin with sleep aids, NyQuil, Benadryl, or prescription sedatives on a night you drink. Treat Claritin-D with more caution, especially if you have heart or blood pressure problems. And if you flush red, break out in hives, or get wheezy when you drink, don't use antihistamines to hide it; see a doctor.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before combining Claritin and alcohol if** you have liver or kidney disease, take other medicines that cause drowsiness (sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, muscle relaxants, seizure medicines), are pregnant or breastfeeding, are over 65, or use Claritin-D and have high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, or trouble urinating. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US)** if someone who mixed alcohol with medicines is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, confused, or has chest pain, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, or a seizure. For questions about a possible overdose, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## How Claritin Works and Why Alcohol Matters at All

Claritin is a brand name. The drug inside it is **loratadine**, a "second-generation" antihistamine used for hay fever, year-round allergies, and hives. The standard adult dose is one 10 mg tablet once a day. Store brands sold as "loratadine" or "non-drowsy allergy relief" contain exactly the same drug.

Antihistamines work by blocking **H1 receptors**, the docking spots that histamine uses to cause sneezing, a runny nose, itchy eyes, and hives. The problem with the older antihistamines, like diphenhydramine (Benadryl), is that they also cross easily into the brain. In the brain, histamine helps keep you awake and alert. Block it there and you get drowsiness, slower reactions, and fuzzy thinking. That's why Benadryl is also sold as a sleep aid.

Loratadine was designed to stay mostly out of the brain. It doesn't cross the blood-brain barrier well, and the brain actively pumps much of what does get in back out again. That's the main reason it's labeled "non-drowsy."

Alcohol matters because it's a **central nervous system depressant**. It slows brain activity on its own, through different pathways from antihistamines. When you combine two things that each nudge your brain toward sleepiness, the effects can add together. With Benadryl that addition is large and genuinely risky. With loratadine at the normal dose, it's usually small. "Usually small" is the honest description: not zero, not dramatic.

### What's different about the Claritin label

If you've read our guide to [Zyrtec and alcohol](/never-hungover/zyrtec-and-alcohol), you may remember that the Zyrtec label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks. The standard Claritin Drug Facts label in the US is worded differently. It doesn't list alcohol among its warnings, and its drowsiness note is tied to dose: taking more than directed may cause drowsiness. It also tells people with liver or kidney disease to ask a doctor before use, because a different dose may be needed.

Label wording changes over time and differs between products, so check the Drug Facts box on your own package, especially for Claritin-D, combination products, or store brands. But the difference in wording reflects a real difference between the drugs: loratadine is less likely than cetirizine to make you sleepy.

## Is Claritin Really Non-Drowsy? What the Research Says

This is where a lot of articles go wrong in one of two directions. Some say Claritin "has no interaction with alcohol at all." Others lump it in with Benadryl. Neither is accurate.

**At the standard dose, loratadine rarely causes sleepiness.** In the clinical trials summarized in its prescribing information, drowsiness was reported only slightly more often with loratadine than with a placebo pill. Reviews comparing the newer antihistamines generally rank loratadine and fexofenadine (Allegra) as the least sedating, with cetirizine (Zyrtec) somewhat more likely to cause drowsiness.

**Studies with alcohol have been reassuring at normal doses.** Controlled studies from the period when loratadine was being developed tested people's reaction times, coordination, and alertness after alcohol with and without loratadine. In general, loratadine at the standard 10 mg dose did not noticeably worsen alcohol's effects on these tests, while older sedating antihistamines did. Some studies found that higher-than-normal doses began to show more sedation, which matches the label's dose-related warning.

**Individual responses vary.** These were mostly small studies in healthy volunteers drinking moderate amounts. They tell you what's typical, not what will happen to you. Some people are simply more sensitive to antihistamines. Heavy drinking is also a different situation from the modest doses used in research.

The practical takeaway: Claritin is one of the better choices if you need an allergy pill on a day you plan to drink. It is not a license to ignore how you feel, and it doesn't make it safe to drive after drinking.

## Loratadine, Your Liver, and Why Dose Matters

Loratadine is broken down in the liver, mainly by two enzymes called **CYP3A4** and **CYP2D6**, into an active compound called **desloratadine**. (Desloratadine is itself sold as a prescription antihistamine, Clarinex.) Desloratadine lasts a long time in the body, which is part of why one Claritin pill covers a full day.

Three things follow from this:

- **Liver disease raises loratadine levels.** If your liver clears the drug more slowly, it builds up, and higher levels make drowsiness more likely. That's why the label tells people with liver disease to ask a doctor about dosing. If you have liver problems and drink, that's an extra reason to talk to someone first.
- **Some medicines raise loratadine levels.** Drugs that slow CYP3A4, such as the antifungal ketoconazole, the antibiotic erythromycin, and the stomach drug cimetidine, have been shown to raise loratadine levels in the blood. Studies didn't find this caused clinically important problems on its own, but it's one more reason to keep a pharmacist in the loop if you take several medicines.
- **Taking extra doesn't help and raises the drowsiness risk.** One 10 mg tablet a day is the adult dose. Taking two because your allergies are bad, or adding a second loratadine-containing product, pushes you toward the dose range where sedation becomes more likely, and alcohol stacks on top of that.

Unlike acetaminophen (see our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol)), loratadine isn't known for causing liver damage when combined with occasional drinking. The liver point here is about how fast the drug is cleared, not about the drug harming the liver.

## Claritin-D and Alcohol: The Version That Needs More Care

**Claritin-D** combines loratadine with **pseudoephedrine**, a decongestant that shrinks swollen blood vessels in your nose. It comes in a 12-hour version and a 24-hour version. In the US, it's kept behind the pharmacy counter and you need to show ID to buy it, because pseudoephedrine can be used to make methamphetamine.

Pseudoephedrine is a **stimulant**. It narrows blood vessels throughout your body, not just in your nose. That can raise blood pressure and heart rate, cause jitteriness or anxiety, and make it hard to sleep. Its label tells people with heart disease, high blood pressure, thyroid disease, diabetes, or trouble urinating from an enlarged prostate to ask a doctor before use, and to stop taking it if they become nervous, dizzy, or sleepless. It must never be combined with MAO inhibitors, an older class of antidepressant.

Here's how alcohol complicates that:

- **Your heart gets pushed from two sides.** Alcohol often raises heart rate, especially as you drink more and as it wears off. Some people get a pounding or racing heart after drinking even without any medicine. Adding a stimulant can make that worse. Our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains when that's harmless and when it isn't.
- **Your sleep takes a double hit.** Alcohol makes you fall asleep faster but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night. Pseudoephedrine keeps many people awake on its own. Together, they're a recipe for a short, poor night and a worse morning.
- **Mixed signals can hide how impaired you are.** A stimulant can make you feel more alert than you really are, while alcohol is still slowing your reactions and judgment. Feeling "fine" isn't a reliable test.
- **Dehydration adds up.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and decongestants dry out your mouth and nose. Neither helps the next morning.

If you're healthy and take Claritin-D for a stuffy nose, a single drink is unlikely to cause a problem, but this is the version where it makes the most sense to keep drinking minimal or skip it. If you have any heart or blood pressure condition, ask a doctor before mixing the two at all. For a deeper look at the decongestant on its own, see our guide to [Sudafed and alcohol](/never-hungover/sudafed-and-alcohol).

## Claritin vs Zyrtec vs Allegra vs Benadryl With Alcohol

People often search for this because they're standing in the allergy aisle wondering which box is the "safe" one for a night out. Here's a general comparison. It's about drowsiness and the main concern with alcohol, not about which works best for your allergies.

| Medicine (drug) | Type | Drowsiness at normal dose | Main concern with alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claritin (loratadine) | Second-generation | Low | Mild extra drowsiness in some people; more likely at higher doses or with liver disease |
| Allegra (fexofenadine) | Second-generation | Low | Similar to Claritin; also avoid taking it with fruit juice, which reduces absorption |
| Zyrtec (cetirizine) | Second-generation | Low to moderate | More likely than Claritin to cause noticeable drowsiness; label says to avoid alcohol |
| Benadryl (diphenhydramine) | First-generation | High | Strong combined sedation and impairment; a poor match with alcohol |
| "-D" versions (Claritin-D, Zyrtec-D, Allegra-D) | Antihistamine plus pseudoephedrine | Varies | Heart rate, blood pressure, jitteriness, and sleep problems on top of the antihistamine |

A few notes:

- **First-generation antihistamines hide in lots of products.** Diphenhydramine and doxylamine show up in "PM" pain relievers, sleep aids, and night-time cold medicines. If you take Claritin in the day and then a night-time cold product after drinking, you may be getting a much more sedating antihistamine than you realize. Our guides to [NyQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol) and [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) cover those in detail.
- **Don't double up on antihistamines.** Taking Claritin and Zyrtec together, or Claritin plus a night-time product, adds side effects without adding much benefit.

## Taking Claritin Before Drinking: Stuffy Nose, Hives, and Red Face

A lot of people search "Claritin and alcohol" because drinking itself sets off allergy-like symptoms. Wine makes their nose run, beer gives them a blotchy rash, or their face goes red after one glass. Claritin can help with some of this, but not all of it, and it's worth knowing the difference.

### When histamine is the problem

Alcohol can trigger the release of histamine in your body, and some drinks, especially red wine and some beers, contain histamine and related compounds of their own. Alcohol may also slow the enzyme that breaks histamine down. In people who are sensitive, that can mean a stuffy or runny nose, sneezing, itchy skin, or hives after drinking.

If those are your symptoms, an antihistamine like loratadine may take the edge off. That's a reasonable use, but notice what it's telling you: your body reacts to something in alcohol, and it's worth figuring out what. Our guides to [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) and [alcohol allergy](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy) walk through the possible causes, from sulfites to histamine to true allergies to grains or other ingredients.

### When it isn't: alcohol flush

The classic "Asian flush" (red face, neck, and chest, often with a fast heartbeat and nausea after small amounts of alcohol) is mostly not a histamine problem. It's usually caused by a common genetic variant in the enzyme **ALDH2**, which leaves a toxic by-product of alcohol called **acetaldehyde** building up in your blood. The redness is a symptom of that buildup.

Some people take antihistamines before drinking to make the redness less visible. That can partly work, but it only hides the color. The acetaldehyde is still there, and research has linked the ALDH2 variant combined with regular drinking to a higher risk of esophageal cancer. Hiding the flush can make it easier to drink more than your body handles well. If you flush, the useful move is to drink less, not to mask it.

### When to stop and see a doctor

Don't try to manage these with Claritin alone. Get medical help if drinking ever causes:

- Swelling of your lips, tongue, face, or throat
- Wheezing, shortness of breath, or tightness in your chest
- Hives spreading over large areas of your body
- Dizziness or faintness along with any of the above

Those can be signs of a serious allergic reaction. Call 911 (in the US) for breathing trouble or throat swelling. A non-drowsy antihistamine is not a treatment for anaphylaxis.

## Can You Take Claritin for a Hangover?

There is no good evidence that Claritin helps with a hangover. A hangover is driven mainly by dehydration, disrupted sleep, low-grade inflammation, irritation of the stomach, and the after-effects of acetaldehyde. Loratadine doesn't target any of those in a meaningful way.

Where it might help is narrow: if part of your morning-after misery is a blocked nose, sneezing, or itchy skin that seems tied to what you drank, your normal dose of Claritin may ease that specific symptom. It won't touch your headache, nausea, or fatigue.

If you take Claritin every day for allergies, keep taking it as usual the morning after drinking. Drink water, eat something, and don't double up. If you're looking for a hangover approach that actually addresses causes, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

### What about Claritin-D for a hangover?

It's a poor choice. If you're dehydrated, shaky, and your heart is already beating faster than usual, adding a stimulant decongestant is more likely to make you feel worse. Save it for genuine congestion.

## How Long After Claritin Can You Drink?

There is no official waiting period, and here's why a waiting time doesn't help much: Claritin is designed to work for 24 hours. Its active by-product, desloratadine, sticks around even longer. Waiting three or four hours after your morning pill doesn't clear it from your system.

So the useful question isn't "how long should I wait," it's "how do I drink sensibly while I'm on it." For most healthy adults on plain Claritin:

- **Take your normal dose at your normal time.** Don't skip it to make room for drinking, and don't take extra.
- **Start slowly.** Have one drink, wait, and notice whether you feel sleepier, dizzier, or more affected than usual.
- **Eat and drink water.** Food slows alcohol absorption, and water helps with the dryness both alcohol and antihistamines can cause.
- **Don't drive.** This is true after drinking anyway, but it's worth repeating when you've added any medicine.

For **Claritin-D**, timing matters a bit more because of the decongestant. The 12-hour version wears off sooner than the 24-hour version. If you want to drink, waiting until the pseudoephedrine dose has run its course is the more cautious choice, and many people simply skip the "-D" on days they plan to drink.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You should talk to a doctor or pharmacist before combining Claritin with alcohol if you:

- **Have liver disease or kidney disease.** Both can raise loratadine levels, and your doctor may want a lower dose.
- **Take other sedating medicines.** That includes sleep aids, anxiety medicines like benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, muscle relaxants, some antidepressants, and seizure medicines. The real risk with alcohol usually comes from these, with Claritin adding a little on top.
- **Use Claritin-D and have heart disease, high blood pressure, an irregular heartbeat, thyroid disease, diabetes, glaucoma, or an enlarged prostate.**
- **Are over 65.** Older adults tend to be more sensitive to drowsiness and falls.
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** Medicine choices during pregnancy are individual, and alcohol has its own guidance.
- **Drink heavily on a regular basis.** At that point the medicine isn't the main issue; regular heavy drinking affects how your liver handles many drugs.

For a broader look at how common medicines interact with supplements and alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## When to See a Doctor or Get Help

Most people who have a drink while on Claritin notice nothing at all. But get help if you see any of these:

**Call 911 (US) or go to the emergency room if** someone who mixed alcohol and medicines:

- Is very hard to wake or can't stay awake
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly
- Is confused, has slurred speech out of proportion to what they drank, or has a seizure
- Has chest pain, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, or fainting (more likely with Claritin-D)
- Has swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if** someone took more than the labeled dose of Claritin or Claritin-D, especially together with alcohol, even if they seem fine.

**Book a regular appointment if** you get hives, flushing, congestion, or wheezing every time you drink, or if you find yourself needing an allergy pill to get through a night out. Those patterns are worth a proper diagnosis.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that some people take around drinking. It's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's best described as promising, not proven.

To be clear about what it doesn't do: DHM is not an antihistamine, it won't treat allergies or alcohol-triggered hives or congestion, and there's no good evidence that it changes how loratadine or pseudoephedrine interact with alcohol. It doesn't make it safer to drive or to mix alcohol with sedating medicines.

If you're interested in trying it alongside sensible drinking habits, it hasn't been shown to interact with loratadine, but check with a pharmacist if you take several medicines. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Plain Claritin (loratadine) at the normal 10 mg dose is one of the least sedating allergy medicines, and light drinking on it is generally fine for healthy adults.
- "Non-drowsy" isn't "zero drowsy." Some people still feel sleepy, especially at higher doses or with liver disease, and alcohol adds to that.
- Claritin-D adds pseudoephedrine, which raises heart rate and blood pressure and disrupts sleep. It deserves more caution with alcohol, and a doctor's input if you have heart or blood pressure problems.
- Never stack Claritin with sleep aids, NyQuil, Benadryl, or prescription sedatives on a night you drink.
- Claritin can ease histamine-driven stuffiness or hives from drinking, but it doesn't fix alcohol flush and there is no good evidence it helps a hangover.
- If drinking causes swelling, wheezing, or widespread hives, get medical help rather than reaching for another pill.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Claritin?**

For most healthy adults, a drink or two while taking a normal 10 mg daily dose of Claritin (loratadine) is unlikely to cause problems. Loratadine is one of the least sedating allergy medicines, and studies at the standard dose have generally not shown it adding much to alcohol's effects. It isn't zero risk, though. Some people still get drowsy, and alcohol is a sedative. Keep drinking light, don't drive until you know how you feel, and ask a pharmacist first if you take other sedating medicines or have liver or kidney disease.

**Is loratadine and alcohol a dangerous combination?**

At the normal 10 mg dose, loratadine and alcohol are not considered a dangerous combination for healthy adults. The concern is mild extra drowsiness, which is less likely than with Zyrtec and much less likely than with Benadryl. The risk goes up if you take more than directed, have liver disease (which slows how fast loratadine is cleared), or also take sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, or other sedatives.

**Can you drink alcohol with Claritin-D?**

Claritin-D deserves more caution than plain Claritin. Besides loratadine, it contains pseudoephedrine, a decongestant that raises heart rate and blood pressure and can cause jitteriness and trouble sleeping. Alcohol can also raise heart rate and disrupt sleep, so the two can add up to a racing heart and a bad night. If you have high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid problems, or diabetes, ask a doctor before using Claritin-D at all, and especially before drinking on it.

**How long after taking Claritin can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period. Claritin is a once-a-day pill whose effect lasts about 24 hours, so waiting a few hours doesn't take it out of your system. For most people, the practical approach is to take your usual dose, drink lightly, and see how you feel before having more. If you take Claritin-D, waiting until the decongestant has worn off (about 12 or 24 hours depending on the version) is the more cautious choice.

**Does Claritin help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that Claritin helps with a hangover. Hangovers come mainly from dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, and the by-products of breaking down alcohol, and an antihistamine doesn't address those. It may ease a stuffy nose or itchy skin after drinking if histamine is part of the picture, but it won't fix the headache, nausea, or fatigue.

**Can Claritin stop a red face or stuffy nose from drinking?**

Claritin can reduce some histamine-driven symptoms, like a stuffy nose, sneezing, or hives after wine or beer. It does not fix alcohol flush caused by a genetic problem breaking down acetaldehyde, and using antihistamines to hide flushing hides a warning sign without removing the toxin behind it. If you flush, get hives, or feel short of breath when you drink, talk to a doctor rather than covering it up.

**Is Claritin safer than Zyrtec or Benadryl with alcohol?**

In terms of drowsiness, yes, generally. Benadryl (diphenhydramine) is strongly sedating and a poor match for alcohol. Zyrtec (cetirizine) is a modern antihistamine but causes drowsiness in more people. Claritin (loratadine) and Allegra (fexofenadine) are the least sedating at normal doses. Less sedating is not the same as risk-free, and Claritin-D brings its own heart and blood pressure concerns.

**Can I take Claritin the morning after drinking?**

Yes, for most healthy adults it's fine to take your normal daily Claritin the morning after a night of drinking. Drink water and eat something too. If you feel unusually drowsy, dizzy, or unwell, rest rather than driving, and don't double up on your dose to make up for anything.
